turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: One hundred and forty-nine! Good heavens! I trust you haven’t been indulging in any… *unsuitable* entertainments within that address? One must be exceedingly careful, you know, about the company one keeps, even when residing in a temporary lodging.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: My dear Lady Bracknell, I can assure you, nothing of the sort has ever occurred! I endeavour to lead a perfectly respectable life, and my intentions are, naturally, always entirely honourable.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Honourable intentions are, of course, a desirable attribute, Mr. Worthing, but they do not, I think, entirely absolve one from scrutiny. Tell me, are your intentions entirely *unconnected* with any previous… attachments? One simply cannot be too diligent in these matters.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Previous attachments? Good heavens, Lady Bracknell, I’m quite sure you’ll find my history perfectly… uncomplicated. I’ve never been involved in anything of that nature, I assure you.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Uncomplicated, you say? A most convenient term, Mr. Worthing, and one I shall endeavour to remember. However, simplicity in a gentleman’s history, while agreeable, does not necessarily equate to suitability. I find myself compelled to inquire, what, precisely, occupies your time? One cannot, you understand, expect a man to subsist solely on honourable intentions.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: My time, Lady Bracknell? Well, I dedicate a good portion to… to civic duties, you see. And, er, tending to my ward, Miss Cecily Cardew. I find it a most rewarding occupation, I do.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Civic duties, you say? Most commendable, Mr. Worthing, though I confess I find myself intrigued by this 'rewarding occupation' involving Miss Cardew. Pray, elaborate; one must ascertain the nature of these duties, and indeed, the precise relationship you maintain with this young lady.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: The nature of my duties, Lady Bracknell? Well, I oversee her education, of course, and ensure she has everything a young lady could possibly require. It’s a responsibility I take very seriously, I can assure you.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A responsibility, you say? How very laudable, Mr. Worthing, but hardly sufficient to dispel my anxieties. I trust, of course, that these ‘duties’ do not involve any… *romantic* entanglements? Such a development would, naturally, be most regrettable.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Romantic entanglements, Lady Bracknell? Oh, no, absolutely not! Miss Cardew is but a child, you see, and I am her guardian. I would never… I would never permit such a thing.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A guardian, you insist? Mr. Worthing, I find myself increasingly perplexed by your pronouncements. One does not simply 'oversee' a young lady’s education without, I daresay, encountering certain… affections. Pray, do not insult my intelligence with further denials.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I assure you, my intentions towards Miss Cardew are entirely paternal and protective. She is, as I said, a young lady under my care, and my focus is solely on her well-being and proper upbringing. I would never, *ever*, dream of anything beyond that.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, your protestations, while vehement, do little to alleviate my concerns. It appears I am dealing with a gentleman of considerable… elasticity in his declarations. Tell me, sir, what is your profession?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: My profession, Lady Bracknell? Well, I… I manage estates, you see. Quite a responsibility, ensuring everything runs smoothly. I consider myself a man of business, primarily.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A man of business, you say? How very… utilitarian. I trust, Mr. Worthing, that your business acumen extends to matters of inheritance and social standing, rather than, say, the breeding of prize-winning poultry?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Prize-winning poultry? Good heavens, no, Lady Bracknell! My interests lie primarily in… well, in land and property, of course. It's a rather… respectable pursuit, I assure you.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mamma! Really, this is quite tedious. Mr. Worthing has clearly demonstrated his… *respectability*, as you seem so concerned with. I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, you know.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Gwendolen, really! Your impatience is quite unbecoming. Mr. Worthing, it appears we are at an impasse; a man of business, you claim, yet your accounts of your business are distressingly vague. I must insist on a more detailed exposition, lest I conclude that your ‘respectability’ is merely a façade.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: A façade, Lady Bracknell? I assure you, I am quite… genuinely respectable! Perhaps I haven't been entirely clear; my responsibilities involve managing the Cecily Cardew estate, which requires a certain… attention to detail, you see.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: The Cecily Cardew estate, you say? My dear Mr. Worthing, one’s responsibilities should always be carefully vetted, naturally. Pray, tell me, who is this Miss Cardew, and what connection does she bear to your… respectable pursuits?

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
